text: This chapter has built up the pieces one at a time: networks, layers, IP addresses, subnets. This lesson is where it all comes together and actually moves traffic, through two devices that do almost all of the work — the switch and the router.

A switch connects devices within the same subnet — in Northbridge's warehouse, every scanner and access point plugs into a switch port. It operates at layer two, forwarding by MAC address. When it powers on it doesn't know who's where; it learns by watching traffic, building a table of which address showed up on which port, then forwards directly instead of blasting every frame everywhere.

A router connects separate subnets or networks together — the device that lets Northbridge's warehouse, office, and guest Wi-Fi subnets reach each other, and the whole site reach the internet. It operates at layer three, forwarding by IP address, using a routing table of known destinations. When nothing more specific matches, it falls back to a default route, typically the path out to the internet.

Here's the full decision when a laptop needs to reach the cloud order database. First, it checks whether the destination is on its own subnet — it isn't, so it sends to its default gateway, the router. The router checks its routing table for the best match. If it's another Northbridge subnet, it forwards there directly. If not, it sends it out the default route, and the packet keeps hopping until it arrives.
That closes out this chapter's foundation — devices, layers, addresses, subnets, switching, and routing, the full picture of how traffic actually moves, all in place before the course moves on.
